unit: modelling
node: AC9M8M07 n2
uses: [AC9M8M07 n1]
title: Checking a model
summary: "Every model makes assumptions: a steady speed with no stops, a fare with no starting charge, an exchange rate with no fees. When a model's answer and real life differ, look for the assumption that does not hold, then refine the model, for example by adding a fixed starting amount."
language: maths
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
connection: electricity-plan   # data/connections/maths.yml; the paper task uses recipe-scaling
hook: "A map app says the drive takes 3 hours. It takes 3 and a half. The maths was right; the model was too simple. Finding out why is the last step of modelling."
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8321
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8321/index.html
  readySelector: "#gsum"
  layout: full
explainPicture: { ref: models.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A taxi fare: $4.20 to start, then $2.10 per km. A 5 km ride costs $4.20 + $10.50 = $14.70." }
explainClip:
  query: { code: "@models.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "A simple model"
  say: "This model only uses the rate per kilometre."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "The simple model: $2.10 per km. 5 km costs $10.50.", say: "The simple model. Two dollars ten per kilometre." }
    - wait: 1200
    - caption: { text: "But this taxi's fare starts at $4.20 before you move. What is missing?", say: "But this taxi's fare starts at four dollars twenty. What is missing?" }
    - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "$10.50" }
    - wait: 1500
---
A **model** is a simplified version of a real situation. Every model makes **assumptions**: things it takes to be true to keep the maths simple.

| Model | Assumption | What can go wrong |
|---|---|---|
| time = distance ÷ speed | a steady speed, no stops | traffic and breaks make it slower |
| water bill = rate × litres | no fixed charge | bills add a service charge |
| US dollars = 0.65 × Australian dollars | no fees, a fixed rate | banks charge fees; rates change daily |

To **review** a model: compare its answer with real life, name the assumption that does not hold, and **refine** the model (add the stop, the fee, whatever was left out). A simple model is fine when the difference does not matter for the decision. The fares and the exchange rate in this lesson are made up for the task.

## Predict: the taxi fare

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to why a simple fare model is wrong shows whether they look for a missing part of the model rather than an arithmetic slip."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A model says a 5 km taxi ride costs 5 × $2.10 = $10.50. The real fare is $14.70. Why?"
  options: ["The model leaves out a starting charge", "5 × 2.10 is not 10.50", "The taxi went faster than expected", "Taxi fares are random"]
  actual: "The model leaves out a starting charge (a flag fall) of $4.20: 4.20 + 10.50 = 14.70. The arithmetic was fine."
```

## Run: the refined model

```step
stage: run
insight: "Moving along the refined fare line shows the fixed start and the rate working together."
try: { playground: board, starter: "models.yml#run", height: 520 }
check: { type: board, text: "This model adds the $4.20 start. Set the ride to 5 km. Was your prediction right?", when: "x = 5", explain: "4.20 + 2.10 × 5 = $14.70." }
```

## Investigate: assumptions

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Name the assumption behind a model; a mismatch is usually the assumption, not the arithmetic (Sam blames the maths); refine by adding what was left out."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A model says a 300 km trip takes 300 ÷ 100 = 3 hours. What does it assume?"
      options: ["The car travels at exactly 100 km/h the whole way, with no stops", "The road is straight", "The car uses no petrol", "Nothing: it is exact"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Bends matter only if they change the speed.", "Petrol is not part of this model.", "Every model assumes something."]
      explain: "Steady speed, no stops, no traffic."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#sam"
      text: "Sam's model and the real trip disagree. Click the line where his review goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: model-blame-maths
      explain: "Line 3: 300 ÷ 100 = 3 is right. The assumption (a steady 100 km/h with no stops) did not hold. Refine the model: add the stops, or use a lower average speed."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "How could you refine the trip model?"
      options: ["Add the time for a stop, or use a lower average speed", "Divide 300 by 100 again", "Make the trip shorter", "Use 3.14 instead of 3"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The same calculation gives the same answer.", "That changes the trip, not the model.", "π has nothing to do with it."]
      explain: "Add what the model left out: a 30-minute stop makes it 3.5 hours."
```

### The trip

Here is the routine.

```worked
\text{model: water bill} = \$2.50 \times \text{kL} :: A simple model: 20 kL costs \$50.
\text{real bill: } \$80 :: Compare with what happened.
\text{assumption: no fixed charge} :: Name what the model took to be true.
\$30 + \$2.50 \times 20 = \$80 :: Refine: add the \$30 service charge.
```

### Find the mistake

Read Sam's review. Is the arithmetic wrong, or the model?

### Refine it

## Modify: refine and judge

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Using the refined fare model backwards, naming a hidden assumption, adding stops, and judging when a simple model is enough."
try: { playground: board, starter: "models.yml#run", height: 520 }
tasks:
  - starter: "models.yml#run"
    hint: ["Take off the $4.20 first.", "21.00 ÷ 2.10 = ?"]
    check: { type: board, text: "With the refined model, how far can you ride for $25.20?", when: "x = 10", explain: "25.20 − 4.20 = 21.00, and 21.00 ÷ 2.10 = 10 km." }
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A money model says 500 Australian dollars buys 500 × 0.65 = 325 US dollars. At the airport you get 305. What assumption failed?"
      options: ["No fees: the exchange counter charges a fee or a worse rate", "500 × 0.65 is not 325", "US dollars are worth more", "The model should divide"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The arithmetic is right.", "Not a reason for the gap.", "Multiplying is right for this direction."]
      explain: "The model ignores fees and the counter's own rate."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "Refine the trip model: 300 km at 100 km/h, plus two 15-minute stops. How many hours does it take?"
      answer: 3.5
      tolerance: 0
      explain: "3 hours driving + 0.5 hours of stops = 3.5 hours."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "When is the simple trip model (300 ÷ 100 = 3 hours) good enough?"
      options: ["For a rough plan, such as which day to travel", "For a train timetable to the minute", "Never", "Only if the answer is a whole number"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A timetable needs more detail.", "Simple models are useful when precision does not matter.", "Whole numbers have nothing to do with it."]
      explain: "A model is good enough when its error does not change the decision."
```

## Practise: checking models

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Assumptions, refined models and a unit-rate review, mixed; blaming the arithmetic for a model's mismatch is the planted slip."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A model for a phone plan is cost = $0.10 per MB used. The real bill was $20 more than the model said. Jo says: 'The model's sum must be wrong.' What is more likely?"
      options: ["The model leaves out a fixed $20 monthly fee", "Jo is right: the sum is wrong", "The price per MB changed", "The phone company made a mistake"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Check the sum first: it is right. A steady $20 gap points to something left out.", "Then the gap would not be exactly $20 every month.", "Possible, but a fixed gap points to a missing fixed charge."]
      explain: "A gap of the same amount every time suggests a fixed charge: cost = 20 + 0.10 × MB."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "With the refined taxi model ($4.20 plus $2.10 per km), what does an 8 km ride cost, in dollars?"
      answer: 21
      tolerance: 0
      feedback:
        - ["16.8", "Add the $4.20 starting charge."]
      explain: "4.20 + 2.10 × 8 = 4.20 + 16.80 = $21."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "A refined phone model is cost = 20 + 0.10 × MB. What is the cost for 350 MB, in dollars?"
      answer: 55
      tolerance: 0
      explain: "20 + 0.10 × 350 = 20 + 35 = $55."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "Review: a car goes 270 km in 3 hours. What is its average speed in km/h?"
      answer: 90
      tolerance: 0
      explain: "270 ÷ 3 = 90 km/h."
```

## Make: a plumber's quote

```step
stage: make
insight: "Using a refined model (a call-out fee plus a rate) backwards, then naming its assumptions."
try: { playground: board, starter: "models.yml#plumber", height: 520 }
hint: ["Take off the $80 call-out first.", "380 ÷ 95 = ?"]
check: { type: board, text: "A plumber charges $80 to come out, then $95 per hour. Find the job length that costs $460.", when: "y = 460", explain: "460 − 80 = 380, and 380 ÷ 95 = 4 hours." }
```

Then name one assumption in the plumber's model, and say how a real bill might differ.

## Make: a camp recipe on paper

```step
stage: make
insight: "Scaling a recipe is a ratio model that works for the ingredients and fails for the bake time; the paper task makes them pick the assumption that breaks and the refinement that fits."
hint: ["Which of the three numbers is about how much, and which is about how long?", "Would a deep dish of 7.5 times the food heat through in the same way?"]
check:
  type: reasoning
  paper: true
  q: "A camp cook has a pasta bake recipe for 4 people: 500 g of pasta, baked for 30 minutes in one dish. The camp needs 30 serves. The cook's model multiplies everything by $30 \\div 4 = 7.5$: 3.75 kg of pasta and 225 minutes in the oven. Review the model."
  steps:
    - ["$30 \\div 4 = 7.5$, so $500 \\times 7.5 = 3750$ g of pasta", "the ingredients do scale in the ratio 30 : 4"]
    - ["$30 \\times 7.5 = 225$ minutes does not follow", "baking time depends on how deep the dish is, not on how many people eat it"]
    - ["Refine: scale the pasta by 7.5, but keep 30 minutes and bake in several dishes as deep as the original", "the model now assumes only what is true: the amounts scale, the time does not"]
  picks:
    - step: 2
      q: "Why does the model go wrong for the baking time?"
      options:
        - "Time is not an amount of food: it depends on the dish, not on the number of serves"
        - "30 × 7.5 is the wrong sum"
        - "The cook should have divided 30 by 4 the other way round"
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The arithmetic is right: 225. The model is what is wrong, not the sum.", "The ratio 30 : 4 is right for the pasta. The trouble is that it was used on the time as well."]
    - step: 3
      q: "What is the best refinement?"
      options:
        - "Scale the amounts by 7.5, keep the time near 30 minutes, and use several dishes"
        - "Scale everything by 7.5 and check the pasta after 100 minutes"
        - "Throw the model out: ratios do not work for recipes"
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That still scales the time. Keep what works (the amounts) and change only what does not.", "The ratio works for the amounts. A model with one wrong assumption is refined, not thrown out."]
  criteria:
    - "I said which parts of the recipe the ratio does scale and which part it does not."
    - "I gave a reason for the part that fails, not just \"it is wrong\"."
    - "My refinement keeps what works and changes only what does not."
  explain: "The amounts scale in the ratio 30 : 4, so 3.75 kg of pasta is a good answer. The time does not: 225 minutes would burn the edges. The refined model scales the amounts, keeps the time, and bakes in several dishes."
```

Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The recipe is made up for the task, but the question is real: caterers scale recipes and then check what the scaling got wrong. Write what the model assumes, which assumption fails, and how you would fix it. The page marks the two reasons you pick.

**Also used in**

- **Energy bills.** Two plans, each a daily charge plus a rate per unit. The comparison assumes the house uses the same amount all year, and summer and winter say otherwise.
- **Travel.** A trip-time model assumes a steady speed with no stops, and every long drive has stops.
- **Money.** An exchange-rate model assumes no fees, until the bank takes its cut.

```teacher
summary: Students compare simple models with real outcomes (taxi fares, trip
  times, exchange rates), name the assumption that failed, and refine the model
  with a starting charge, stops or fees (AC9M8M07, node 2).
time: 35
timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 8 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and
  Make 9 min
goals:
  - I can name an assumption a model makes.
  - I can explain how an assumption makes a model's answer differ from real life.
  - I can refine a model and say when a simple one is good enough.
struggle: Separating the maths from the model. When an answer is 'wrong', ask
  students to check the arithmetic first, then ask what the model took to be
  true.
before: >
  Do the Run board yourself first. Students need rate models (previous lesson).


  The one idea: when a model and real life disagree, look for the assumption
  that did not hold, then refine. The common mistake is blaming correct
  arithmetic (Sam's mistake).


  The board's starting charge (`base`) shows a refined model: a fixed amount
  plus a rate. The taxi fare, plumber's prices and exchange rate are round
  examples, not real tariffs.


  Wider: compare a simple tax model (one rate for everyone) with the bracket
  model from Money models; constant versus changing exchange rates.
running:
  - "Predict: ask whether 5 × 2.10 is right."
  - "Run: ask what the fare is for 0 km."
  - "Investigate: ask Sam to check 300 ÷ 100."
  - "Modify: ask when the simple trip model is fine."
  - "Make: ask for an assumption about the plumber's time."
  - "Paper: the camp recipe is worked in books; the page marks two reasons (why
    the time fails, and the refinement) and has no number answer. Books out,
    then look for which parts of the model were kept."
stuck:
  - see: A student says the maths is wrong.
    ask: Is the calculation right? What did the model assume?
    fix: Check the arithmetic, then name the assumption.
  - see: A student forgets the fixed charge when working backwards.
    ask: What do you pay before the meter starts?
    fix: Take the fixed part off first, then divide by the rate.
  - see: A student cannot name an assumption.
    ask: What would have to be true for the answer to be exact?
    fix: That is the assumption.
stretch: Find a real taxi or rideshare fare structure for your city and build
  its model. What does it still leave out (waiting time, surge pricing)?
support: "A frame: The model assumes … In real life … So the answer … A better
  model would …"
leads: >
  This completes AC9M8M07.


  Where it leads: linear models with a starting value (Linear relations: y = mx
  + c), and modelling in Years 9 and 10.
exit:
  q: A model says 4 kg of apples at $3.50 per kg cost $14. The shop charges $12.60
    for 4 kg. Name a possible assumption that failed.
  a: "A fixed price per kg: the shop may give a discount for buying more (a bulk
    price)."
explain: >
  Every **model** makes **assumptions** (steady speed, no fees, no starting
  charge). When the model and real life differ, check the arithmetic, then name
  the assumption that did not hold.


  **Refine** the model by adding what was left out, such as a starting charge:
  fare = $4.20 + $2.10 × km. A simple model is good enough when its error does
  not change the decision.
```
